name: Ranger 7
intro: After six Ranger missions failed, Ranger 7 finally did it. It dove into the Moon taking pictures all the way down and sent home 4,308 sharp close-ups in its last 17 minutes. Its crater is in a sea later named Mare Cognitum, “the Sea that has become known”.
whyLeft: Rangers were built to crash: they took pictures until they hit the ground at 2.6 km per second.
repurpose: Its crater is a known-age scar, so scientists can use it like a clock to measure how quickly fresh craters darken and fade.
funFact: Ranger 7’s last pictures could show things smaller than 1 m across, about a thousand times finer than the best telescopes on Earth at the time.

hotspots.title: Impact crater
hotspots.text: Ranger 7 hit right here at 2.62 km per second. It was destroyed instantly, leaving a small crater that orbiters have since photographed from above.

hotspots.title: First picture
hotspots.text: Ranger 7’s first picture was taken about 17 minutes before impact, from 2,110 km up. The big crater on the right is Alphonsus, where Ranger 9 would crash eight months later.

photo.alt: A wide view of cratered lunar terrain, the first picture of the Moon from a US spacecraft
photo.caption: The first picture of the Moon ever taken by a US spacecraft, by Ranger 7 on 31 July 1964.
photo.licenseEvidence: JPL Photojournal PIA02975, credit NASA/JPL (NASA, public domain under NASA media guidelines)

hotspots.title: Last pictures
hotspots.text: The last two pictures were taken less than half a second before impact, from about 1 km and 0.5 km up. They are cut off because Ranger 7 smashed into the ground before it finished sending them.

photo.alt: Two close-up pictures of the lunar surface, the lower part filled with static
photo.caption: Ranger 7’s last two pictures, cut off by the impact.
photo.licenseEvidence: NASA NSSDCA Photo Gallery: image returned by NASA’s Ranger 7 (US government work, public domain)

hotspots.title: Craters on craters
hotspots.text: Ranger 7’s close-ups showed that even flat lunar plains are peppered with small craters, some only a few metres across. Planners now knew landers needed to cope with bumpy ground.

photo.alt: A close-up of flat lunar ground covered in small craters
photo.caption: The last picture from Ranger 7’s camera A, taken 2.5 seconds before impact from 6.5 km up.
photo.licenseEvidence: NASA NSSDCA Photo Gallery: image returned by NASA’s Ranger 7 (US government work, public domain)
